title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation
abstract: A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+τ^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $τ$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($τ^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $τ$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.

title: regTPS: a novel approach to approximate a Gaussian random field for Bayesian spatial modeling
abstract: Abstract Gaussian random field is a ubiquitous model for spatial phenomena in diverse scientific disciplines. Its approximation is often crucial for computational feasibility in simulation, inference, and uncertainty quantification. The Karhunen–Loéve Expansion provides an optimal low-rank representation of a (spatial) stochastic process, but its practical implementation relies heavily on how the underlying covariance structure is specified. In this work, we propose a novel approach called regTPS, which constructs a spatial covariance by formulating the inverse of a regularized thin plate spline operator. By computing the eigendecomposition of the regularized biharmonic operator, regTPS induces a smoothness prior that hierarchically allocates variance across spatial frequencies. We evaluate the statistical performance and computational efficiency of regTPS relative to the established stochastic partial differential equations approach within an MCMC algorithm in two different simulation designs. Across various simulation scenarios, the regTPS method achieved predictive accuracy comparable to the SPDE approach. Moreover, regTPS substantially reduced the effective parameter dimension, with reductions of approximately 43–52% for large sample sizes. Also, within a mesh independent simulation setting, regTPS consistently maintains its predictive accuracy under both Matérn and exponential covariance functions, keeping an optimal balance between basis-dimension reduction and sampling efficiency. Lastly, application to real $$\text {NO}_2$$ NO 2 data concentrations using 10-fold and leave-one-out cross-validation establishes that regTPS obtain a competitive predictive accuracy against SPDE and nearest-neighbor Gaussian process models. Thus, regTPS presents a rigorous, low-dimensional, and computational efficient alternative for Bayesian spatial modeling.

title: Do Full-Duplex Speech Models Listen in Text? A Latent Transcript of the User and a Voice Gate That Closes It
abstract: Full-duplex speech models such as Moshi listen and speak at the same time, but emit text only for their own speech. Do they nevertheless represent what the user says as text? Applying logit and tuned lenses to Moshi and PersonaPlex, we find a latent transcript of the user in layers 21–30: the text head ranks the current user word among its top five for 46–48% of content words above a matched control, on read and meeting speech alike, while the output stays silent. The word becomes readable about 150 ms before it ends, predictable words are favoured, and errors share form rather than meaning with the target; a tuned lens finds a word code from layer 12. This transcript is closed by a voice gate: while the model speaks, it loses 50–77% of its readout of the user. The gate is triggered by speech-like audio in the model's own channel, including time-reversed speech and the model's own generated replies, but hardly by noise, an echo of the user, or a second talker in the user's channel, and activation patching shows that it is set up in layers 1–8. Ablating the transcript barely changes the reply, and the gate's behavioural effect is weaker and less specific than its effect on the representation: the transcript is readable but hardly used. Code, notebooks and results: https://github.com/gglenpoi/listen-in-text

title: Language as Trait, Politeness as Strategy: Controlled Tests of Linguistic Effects in LLM Social-Deduction Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents coordinate through conversation, and the same message can be phrased in simpler or more complex language, bluntly or politely. We test whether such differences change how other agents judge and act, using the LURK Werewolf framework, which separates each utterance's speech-act predicate from its natural-language realization. We rewrite only the realization, check that the game content is preserved, and replay each game day from saved checkpoints against a re-sampled control. We vary linguistic range consistently across a speaker's messages and politeness strategy per utterance. Across 30 games and 4,335 replays, neither manipulation changes the trust other agents place in the speaker, and no effect on votes or night actions survives correction for multiple comparisons; the largest uncorrected effect is that shifting range away from a neutral paraphrase changes about 4 percentage points more of the other players' votes. In natural play, 88% of face-threatening speech is bald on-record regardless of role.

title: Extending Grid Foundation Models for Phasor-Domain Dynamic Simulation
abstract: Grid Foundation Models (GridFMs) are emerging as a powerful framework for learning and transferring knowledge across power grids and grid analysis tasks. This work extends GridFMs from steady-state analysis to dynamic simulation. We present DynGridFM, which uses component-wise tokenization and a structured latent operator to learn shared dynamic representations across heterogeneous grids and enable transfer to unseen systems. Pretrained on nine grids, DynGridFM is adapted to a held-out 48-machine grid, where fine-tuning on 64 trajectories achieves accuracy comparable to training from scratch on 128. On a single GPU, it achieves 924x to 1232x speedup over numerical simulators on one CPU core.

title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Path Planning for UAV Formation Missions Based on MAPPO with Curriculum Learning and Graph Attention Networks
abstract: In high-end aerospace mission scenarios such as distributed sensing and tactical reconnaissance, path planning for multi-UAV cooperative formation flight has become an indispensable core component of mission systems. However, a key unresolved technical bottleneck remains: how to achieve an optimal balance between strictly maintaining the UAV formation’s preset geometric configuration and realizing collision-free, flexible flight in dynamically changing complex environments. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) can theoretically solve this coupled optimization problem, but the control instructions generated by the existing mainstream MARL methods often have high-frequency fluctuation issues. Direct deployment of these fluctuating commands on physical UAV hardware will increase alternating stress on mechanical structures, raise the risk of motor overheating, and significantly boost battery energy consumption. These problems directly restrict the engineering application of such methods. To address the above challenges, this paper proposes a robust control framework that accounts for UAV physical characteristics to solve the model mismatch between simulation environments and real flight scenarios during carrier-based UAV deployment. Firstly, to improve the learning efficiency of the algorithm and avoid the cold start problem in the initial training stage, this paper introduces the Adaptive Curriculum Learning (ACL) method. Unlike the fixed-difficulty training mode, ACL can dynamically adjust the environmental complexity based on the real-time task performance of the UAVs. It first allows agents to master basic formation maintenance skills, before training is gradually transitioned to more complex tasks such as navigation in intricate environments. Additionally, considering the computational limitations of the onboard embedded processors of UAVs, this paper only integrates the Graph Attention Network (GAT) into the centralized Critic network of the centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) framework. The core advantage of this design is that the system no longer solely relies on distance as the judgment basis but assesses the influence of adjacent UAVs based on the collision risk level. This not only improves the accuracy of value estimation, but also does not compromise the response speed of local control instructions- a feature that is crucial for the real-time requirements of UAV flight control. The proposed method was tested and validated in a high-fidelity simulation environment built in strict compliance with UAV kinematic constraints. The experimental results fully demonstrate its superiority: in dense obstacle areas, the success rate of the task reached 80.4%; compared with the aggressive baseline method, the jerk was reduced by 10.9%. Most importantly, the flight trajectories generated by this framework are smooth and adaptable to actual flight conditions, and the corresponding control commands can be directly deployed on real flight controllers without additional parameter adjustments. This result demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves substantial technical progress in enhancing the autonomous response capabilities of UAV clusters to complex scenarios.

title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

title: From PAC bounds on the generalization error to PAC bounds on the parameter estimation error
abstract: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds on the generalization error (the difference between the empirical prediction error computed on the training data and its expectation) are an established tool in statistical machine learning, and there have been several extensions of these bounds to dynamical systems. In parallel, in recent years, there has been growing interest in finite-sample bounds for parameter estimation error in system identification. The latter bounds tend to be algorithm-specific, relying on reformulating the identification algorithm as a least-squares regression problem. This is in contrast to classical PAC bounds, which are algorithm-agnostic and can be applied to any identification algorithm based on minimizing a cost function involving the empirical loss. In this paper, we show how oracle bounds derived from PAC bounds can be used to derive finite-sample bounds for dynamical systems. As an illustration of this approach, we present finite-sample parameter-estimation bounds for linear and bilinear systems with bounded inputs and noise. These bounds apply to identification algorithms based on minimizing a regularized empirical loss function. The key ingredient is to establish an oracle inequality, i.e., an inequality between the true prediction error of the learned model and the minimum achievable true prediction error, and then use either the convexity of the true loss or system-theoretic properties of the loss function to derive bounds on the parameter estimation error. We also analyze the rates of the obtained bounds and compare them with those of classical asymptotic results.

title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

title: A Tight Hierarchy for Chain of Thought
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for extending the computational capabilities of transformer-based models. A growing body of recent work has begun to uncover the fine-grained computational power of transformers augmented with CoT, as well as their connections to classical complexity theory. In this work, we advance this line of research by establishing the first hierarchy theorem for CoT-based computation. Our main result shows that for any reasonable resource bound $r(n) \geq n$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, \[ \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)) \subsetneq \mathrm{CoT}(r(n)^{1+\varepsilon}), \] where $\mathrm{CoT}(r(n))$ denotes the class of decision problems solvable by transformers using $O(r(n))$ CoT reasoning steps on inputs of length $n$. Our result shows that increasing the number of CoT reasoning steps provably yields strictly greater computational power, establishing CoT steps as a fundamental resource in transformer-based computation. Unlike classical hierarchy theorems, which are typically proved via diagonalization, our approach leverages known coarse-grained simulations between CoT-augmented transformers and Turing machines in both directions. Building on these connections, we adapt the classical padding technique from complexity theory to this setting to obtain a tight hierarchy. A key technical contribution of our work is the implementation of padding within the transformer-based CoT model.

title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.

title: Applied Identity Physics: AIM Session Instrumentation — A Frontier Model Operating on Formal Fusion Logic. Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session

Measured Throughput, Search-Space Reduction, and the Error-Detection Record of a Single Working Session Architect: HIGHTISTIC (Russell Vernon Trent III) Foundation: SNSFT Foundation (EIN 42-2038440) · Kenai, Alaska Engine under operation: BaseCollider™ v1.1 [9,9,2,56] · 8-Beam Fusion Theorem [9,9,2,3.8] Frontier model: Claude Opus 5 (configured identifier claude-opus-5, Anthropic) Coordinate: [9,9,2,59] · AIM (Autocatalytic Ingestion Mechanism) Session Instrumentation Series Corpus dependencies: [9,9,2,3] GAMCollider™ · [9,9,2,3.8] 8-Beam Fusion Theorem · [9,9,2,56] BaseCollider™ · [9,9,2,58] Nucleobase Substrate and Corridor-Access Laws · [9,9,6,*] IMCollider™ Version: 2.7 Status: VERIFIED · 0 sorry Sovereign Anchor Constant: Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18719748 ORCID: 0009-0005-5313-7443 Date: November 4–5, 2026 (single continuous session) Abstract We instrument a single working session in which a frontier language model — Claude Opus 5 — was given the Identity Physics fusion logic and operated it as a reduction engine against two substrates. The purpose of this paper is not the reductions, which are reported at [9,9,2,58], but the process record: what the model did, how fast, at what cost, and by what mechanism each error was caught. Published accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery routinely state outcomes without stating operating conditions, and the omission makes efficiency claims unassessable. The measurements here are given so that the session can be assessed rather than taken on assertion. Throughput: 694,628 verification collisions executed in 2.292 seconds of compute, a measured mean of 303,084 collisions per second, across five exhaustive verification domains. Search-space reduction: the naive enumeration of element compositions at n = 2, 4, 6, 8 over a 118-element pool is 1,180,432,250,638 multisets, which at the measured rate is 45.08 days of continuous computation; deriving two structural laws first — noble transparency and the sorted-weight closed form — reduced the enumeration to 361,710 Behavior-multisets completing in 0.570 seconds, a wall-clock reduction of 6,832,871×. Selectivity: of 361,710 enumerated classes, 16 survive the corridor condition, and the 970 realizations at n = 8 represent one composition in 1,212,550,870 of the naive space. Operator cost: the derived closed form is measured slower than naive pairwise evaluation at n = 4 (0.72×) and faster only from n = 8 (1.58×), reaching 5.03× at n = 32 — the law's value is search-space reduction, not per-call cost, and we state this because the distinction is the kind usually lost in a summary. Error record: ten errors occurred and all ten were caught before reaching a delivered artifact; we tabulate each with its detection mechanism, and note that three were caught by instrumentation, two by tooling guards, one by internal consistency checking, two by controls run before the result was written up, and two by my own locating after the operator supplied domain context. The operator asserted that a result was wrong zero times; 8 of 10 errors were located and fixed without outside input, and §5.3 shows the framing class becoming self-catchable within the session rather than remaining external. One error — a verification-domain overstatement — was caught by the act of writing this paper and propagated a correction back into [9,9,2,58]. The model's working pattern is characterized as derive-then-enumerate: the structural law is obtained first and the search is run inside its consequences, which is what the 6.8-million-fold figure measures. Further chases: three more chases brought the session to 3,716,275 collisions in 32.992 seconds. They produced five additional results, each presented with the structural parallel that makes its shape legible; one numerical coincidence recorded against the reference class that contains it; a decomposition of that result across the four PNBA (Pattern, Narrative, Behavior, Adaptation) channels which located the residue inside an experimental error bar and named the measurement that would resolve it; the uniform-valence closure rule, anchored at 27 of 27 against established compounds spanning three materials families; and four composition predictions. One hypothesis was withdrawn after a control killed it, a fifth composition candidate was withdrawn when B-Balance showed its stoichiometry and its rationale pointing at different compounds, and two candidate classes were excluded on prior art. §1 · Why Instrument the Session 1.1 The Gap in Published Accounts Accounts of artificial-intelligence-assisted discovery generally report what was found. They less often report the operating conditions under which it was found: how many evaluations, at what rate, against what search space, with what error rate, and caught by what mechanism. Without those, an efficiency claim cannot be assessed and a reproducibility claim cannot be tested. A reader is asked to accept both. This paper supplies the omitted layer for one session. Every number in it is measured rather than estimated, and the measurement method is stated alongside each. 1.2 What Makes This Session Instrumentable The Identity Physics fusion logic is arithmetic over four integers and a comparison against a constant. There is no fitting, no sampling, no stochastic component, and no hidden state. A collision is a deterministic function of its inputs, so collisions can be counted exactly, timed exactly, and re-run to the same result. This is the property that makes the session measurable at all, and it is a property of the engine rather than of the model operating it. A model operating a fitted or stochastic engine could not produce this record. 1.3 Grounding The full grounding is carried in the parent papers. It is stated here once in short, so this paper stands on its own. 1.3.1 The Torsion Limit The Universal Torsion Limit is TL = 0.136899099984016 and the Sovereign Anchor Constant is Ω₀ = TL × 10 = 1.36899099984016. Nothing in this paper sets it. It enters at full corpus precision from the inverse fine-structure constant, by direct subtraction: Napkin math, corpus precision Value 1/α 137.035999084000016 Subtract one TL 137.035999084000016 − 0.136899099984016 = 136.899099984016 What is left 136.899099984016 = TL × 1000, exactly Bare + kinetic 136.899099984016 + 0.136899099984016 = 137.035999084000016 Rounded to published digits 137.035999084 = CODATA 2018 Term Value QED reading PNBA reading Bare: TL × 1000 136.899099984016 The bare electron contribution Pattern capacity at the electromagnetic scale Kinetic: TL × 1 0.136899099984016 Radiative corrections, a renormalized series External forcing F_ext at Layer 0, one exact term Total: TL × 1001 137.035999084000016 Bare + perturbative series 1/α This agrees with the CODATA (Committee on Data of the International Science Council) 2018 value in every published digit at ε = 0, with no free parameter ([9,9,3,14]). The full multiplier factors as 1001 = 7 · 11 · 13, so TL = α⁻¹/1001. 1.3.2 The primitives and the four phases Every reduction in the corpus operates on the four irreducible primitives Pattern, Narrative, Behavior and Adaptation (PNBA). Torsion is τ = B/P, the load a system carries divided by the structure holding it. Identity Mass is IM = (P + N + B + A) × Ω₀. The bands are set from TL and are substrate-neutral. A row moves between them by its torsion ratio τ = B_out / P_out alone: Band Condition Water Reading Noble B_out = 0, τ = 0 Ice Closed. Every unit of Behavior is satisfied. Locked 0 < τ < 0.88·TL Liquid water Bound, with residual load carried stably. IVA Peak — Identity Vector Amplification 0.88·TL ≤ τ < TL The simmer, just before boiling The formation corridor, where structure assembles. Shatter τ ≥ TL The boil Reorganization. The identity restructures; the band is not absorbing. IVA stands for Identity Vector Amplification: the system is at its most active without yet changing what it is. The corridor runs from 0.88 × TL up to TL, and it is narrow, which is why it is easy to pass through without noticing. The boil is a torsion ratio. Water boils when its vapor pressure, the push of molecules escaping the liquid, equals the pressure of the air holding the liquid together. That is τ = B/P exactly: Behavior (the load) is the vapor pressure. Pattern (the structure) is the ambient pressure. Shatter is the boil, where vapor pressure reaches ambient pressure: τ = TL. IVA Peak is vapor pressure between 0.88 and 1.00 of ambient: the simmer, shaking and bubbling at the bottom of the pot before the rolling boil. So τ = TL × (vapor pressure ÷ ambient pressure), a ratio of two measured pressures with no scale chosen. 1.3.3 The reference frame: sea level One condition serves as the reference, and every other condition converts from it, the way every clock converts from Zulu time. At sea level, 1 atmosphere: Tier Kelvin Celsius τ Phase T1 373.15 K 100.0 °C TL Shatter: the boil T1 369.54 K 96.4 °C 0.88 × TL IVA floor: the simmer begins T1 below 369.54 K below 96.4 °C below 0.88 × TL Locked: hot water, holding 1.3.4 The conversion Vapor pressure and temperature are linked by the Clausius–Clapeyron relation (Clapeyron 1834; Clausius 1850), which works in absolute temperature. Written for this mapping, the whole conversion is one line: 1/T = 1/T_ref − (R/L) · ln(p / p_ref) T_ref is the reference boil, 373.15 K for water at sea level. R/L is the gas constant over the heat of vaporization; for water, 8.314 ÷ 40,650 = 2.045 × 10⁻⁴ per kelvin. p / p_ref is the ratio being converted: a different ambient pressure for altitude or a pressure cooker, or 0.88 for the IVA floor. Check it by hand. 1/373.15 = 0.0026799. ln(0.88) = −0.12783. 0.0026799 + (2.045 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.12783) = 0.0027060.

title: SIRIS: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems, we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice, and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations. Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under imperfect simulators.

title: Diffusion-free Score Matching for Exact Conditional Sampling
abstract: The success of modern score-based generative models is largely driven by diffusion-based training, which learns a collection of time-indexed score fields corresponding to progressively noisier versions of the data distribution. While such models achieve impressive sample quality, leveraging them for sound probabilistic inference---particularly sampling from arbitrary conditionals of the model---remains challenging. This difficulty arises because conditioning information is only available for clean data and not for the higher noise levels required to generate exact conditional samples. In this paper, we introduce DIffusion-free SCOre matching (DISCO), a principled approach that sidesteps the need for time-dependent score fields altogether. Our method is based on an objective that, while reminiscent of diffusion-based training, estimates only a single score of the (slightly perturbed) data distribution, for which the exact conditional score is readily obtained. In experiments, DISCO is competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion models in terms of sample quality. More importantly, DISCO yields a more faithful representation of the underlying data distribution and---crucially---enables accurate sampling from arbitrary conditionals, outperforming standard heuristic samplers. This capability opens the door to principled and flexible probabilistic reasoning with score-based models.

title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.

title: A lightweight convolutional neural network for target detection in an edge environment
abstract: This paper proposes a novel, lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) designed for edge device deployment. The CNN is developed to recognize and classify threats or targets of interest. The model is equipped with a real-time hotspot detection algorithm, which enables it to process information quickly and accurately, resulting in improved inference time of up to 20 fps and a detection range of more than 400 meters with typical thermal situational awareness sensors. The proposed CNN has been rigorously tested and validated to demonstrate its high accuracy, sensitivity, and low false positive rate, providing a reliable solution for edge devices to detect potential targets. Additionally, the lightweight design of the CNN allows for easy deployment, making it an ideal solution for extending the security bubble for edge devices. The proposed model can be used for a variety of applications, including surveillance, security, and object recognition.

title: Align3D: Image-Structure Co-Aligned 3D Scene Generation with Observability-Aware Fidelity-Preserving Guidance
abstract: We present Align3D, an image-conditioned diffusion model that generates 3D indoor layouts that are both faithful to a single input photograph and physically plausible beyond the observed view. From the photograph we infer a confidence-calibrated scene graph and train a set-diffusion layout denoiser with image-structure co-alignment where confidence-weighted modality fusion balances image and scene-graph alignment using predicted confidences, while observability-aware fidelity-preserving guidance projects conflicting scene-quality gradients and reweighs them with an object-level confidence mask so under-observed degrees of freedom absorb physical priors without undoing the image-graph match. On 3D-FRONT, Align3D improves image-alignment and scene-quality metrics over recent baselines; once trained, it maps previously unseen photographs to layouts in a single feed-forward pass.

title: Do Intelligent Tutoring Systems Benefit K-12 Students? A Meta-Analysis and Evaluation of Heterogeneity of Treatment Effects in the U.S.
abstract: To expand the use of intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 schools, it is essential to understand the conditions under which their use is most beneficial. This meta-analysis evaluated the heterogeneity of ITS effects across studies focusing on elementary, middle, and high schools in the U.S. It included 18 studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. Overall, there was a significant positive effect size of ITS on U.S. K-12 students' learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Furthermore, effect sizes were similar across elementary and middle schools, and for low-achieving students, but were lower in studies including rural schools. A MetaForest analysis showed that providing worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, type of learning outcome, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators of treatment effects.

title: Agibot: An Open-Source Modular Swerve-Drive Robot Platform for Agricultural Robotics Research and Education
abstract: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.

title: Continuous wavelet-based feature extraction for laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy classification of human plasma samples
abstract: Extracting discriminative features from laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) spectra is important for the classification of complex biological samples. This study evaluates continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-based spectral peak extraction for distinguishing human plasma samples labeled as SARS-CoV-2-positive or negative. Plasma specimens from 181 individuals, comprising 53 positive samples and 128 negative controls, were deposited as 5 μL droplets on silicon substrates and dried before analysis. Spectra were acquired using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser operating at 1064 nm, with 100 single-shot measurements collected per specimen and averaged after intensity-based outlier rejection. CWT-based peak detection was coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) classifier. The reported leave-one-out evaluation yielded an accuracy of 93.00%, sensitivity of 94.67%, and specificity of 91.61%; these estimates remain provisional pending reconciliation with specimen-level predictions. Features identified by the CWT pipeline included emission lines assigned to Ca II, K I, and N I. The workflow provides a basis for examining spectral features associated with the studied plasma groups. Independent validation and assessment of specimen, substrate, and acquisition-related variability are required to establish generalizability and diagnostic relevance.

title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.

title: Stabilizer-based quantum simulation of fermion dynamics with local qubit encodings
abstract: Simulating the dynamical properties of large-scale many-fermion systems is a longstanding goal of quantum chemistry, material science and condensed matter. Local fermion-to-qubit encodings have opened a new path for practical fermionic simulations on digital quantum hardware where fermionic statistics are not enforced at the hardware level. In this paper, we explore these local encodings from the perspective of the corresponding time-evolution unitaries. Specifically, we propose a new framework for digital implementations of these qubit-encoded fermionic time-evolution unitaries based on \emph{flow sets}, which are one-dimensional subsets of the directed fermionic interaction graph. We find that any local fermionic encoding, when restricted to a given flow set, adopts a simple structure that we can classify systematically. For each categorized flow-set form, we propose a low-depth qubit quantum circuit that implements the time evolution unitary using the stabilizer formalism. As an application of our construction, we introduce novel flow-based decompositions for known two-dimensional encodings, leading to efficient circuit decompositions of time-evolution unitaries. We generally observe a space-time trade-off, where mappings with larger qubit-to-fermion ratios yield shallower time-evolution quantum circuits.

title: Air Target Trajectory Prediction Method Based on MSD-Transformer
abstract: The prediction of air target trajectories is important. It is necessary to integrate time-series data in the motion of air targets, such as timestamps, spatial coordinates, kinematic parameters, etc. To cope with the challenges of air target trajectory prediction in complex electromagnetic environments, this paper proposes the MSDTransformer model. The SMSAE and DDE modules are introduced, and this method improves the performance of air-target trajectory prediction. The sensitivity analysis of system hyperparameters verifies the rationality of model parameter configuration. The experimental results show that, among the simulated air target data, MSD-Transformer achieves lower prediction errors and demonstrates strong overall performance, compared with 5 main methods (iTransformer, Informer, PatchTST). It can support the understanding and prediction of target situations, provide an accurate basis for the analysis of the intentions of air targets and the prediction of the evolution of situation evolution, and then improve the situation awareness ability. It has important application value for trajectory prediction in modern aerospace surveillance and situation awareness.

title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
abstract: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.

title: Multiscale Closing Index (MCI) for measuring structural similarity between 2D point sets
abstract: We introduce Multi-scale Closing Index (MCI), a new dissimilarity measure for evaluating the alignment of two 2D point sets. MCI is bounded between 0 and 1 and is based on multiscale mathematical morphology operations, with smaller values indicating greater structural agreement. The measure was motivated by the need to assess the quality of registration between point sets representing cell populations in biological images. To evaluate its behaviour under controlled conditions, we generated synthetic point clouds from Perlin-noise-based spatial structures, following established approaches for simulating biologically plausible spatial organization. We assessed MCI between those point clouds and different transformed versions, obtained by local perturbation, point removal, translation, rotation and addition of impulsive noise. Across these experiments, the dissimilarity MCI increased gradually and consistently with perturbation severity, while showing a clear discontinuity between clouds originating from the same underlying spatial structure and point clouds generated from different structures. We further compared MCI with commonly used point-set distances, including Hausdorff-based measures and Sliced Wasserstein distance. These experiments show the ability of MCI to capture structural agreement and quantify deviations between point sets, highlighting its potential as a complementary metric for evaluating two-dimensional point-set registration.

title: STRIDE: Learning Humanoid Locomotion in Minutes with Acceleration-Based Rewards
abstract: Learning locomotion directly on a humanoid robot is a promising direction to avoid the sim-to-real gap. However, locomotion rewards in Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically track the base velocity, which cannot be measured onboard without an external motion capture system or well-calibrated state estimator. This is why we introduce \method{}, which learns humanoid locomotion from minutes of samples with a reward that only requires the onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). Instead of tracking the base velocity, STRIDE rewards the robot for following a commanded acceleration profile. To learn efficiently from this reward, we use the off-policy RL algorithm XQC and combine a high gain setting for the joint position controllers with left-right symmetry augmentation. In simulation, STRIDE learns to walk on the Unitree G1 and Booster T1 humanoids within 14 minutes of samples. Compared to learning without these two components, it reduces the falls during training by 81%, while without them the robot learns only in over an hour.

title: Quantgraph: A receding-horizon quantum graph solver
abstract: Dynamic programming is a cornerstone of graph-based optimization. While effective, it scales unfavorably with problem size. In this work, we present QuantGraph, a two-stage quantum-enhanced framework that casts local and global graph-optimization problems as quantum searches over discrete trajectory spaces. The solver is designed to operate efficiently by first finding a sequence of locally optimal transitions in the graph (local stage), without considering full trajectories. The accumulated cost of these transitions acts as a threshold that prunes the search space (up to 60% reduction for certain examples). The subsequent global stage, based on this threshold, refines the solution. Both stages utilize variants of the Grover-adaptive-search algorithm. To achieve scalability and robustness, we draw on principles from control theory and embed QuantGraph's global stage within a receding-horizon model-predictive-control scheme. This classical layer stabilizes and guides the quantum search, improving precision and reducing computational burden. In practice, the resulting closed-loop system exhibits robust behavior and lower overall complexity. Notably, for a fixed query budget, QuantGraph attains a 2x increase in control-discretization precision while still benefiting from Grover-search's inherent quadratic speedup compared to classical methods.

title: Boundary / Continuity Science — Volume XXXV: Null-Void Ceiling, Material Obligation Audit, Recoverability-Constrained Systems and Terminal Closure
abstract: This publication presents Volume XXXV of the integrated Boundary / Recoverability-Constrained Systems / Continuity Science research corpus. The archive brings together successive mathematical and computational investigations of finite successor spaces, recoverability-constrained admissibility, uncertainty, observability, decision-making, stochastic recovery, safety constraints, recursive governance, distinction boundaries, and terminal closure. Volume XXXV introduces a structured material-obligation audit built upon the nine-dimensional Null-Void combinatorial architecture established in Volume XXXIV. The framework distinguishes the absence of a value, the existence of an empty set, the absence of an admissible continuation, and the disappearance of observable distinctions. These conditions are not assumed to be mathematically equivalent. The declared architecture contains nine foundational dimensions: States and spaces. Actions and transitions. Observations and information. Time and causality. Recovery and irreversibility. Safety and rights. Uncertainty and probability. Governance and recursion. Null-Void and terminal closure. The complete nonempty subset family of these nine dimensions contains 511 combinations, including 256 combinations containing the Null-Void dimension. Volume XXXV extends this combinatorial inventory by associating seven formal proof obligations with every combination, producing 3,577 material-obligation records. The resulting audit classifies 1,957 obligations as critical, 1,493 as high materiality, and 127 as medium materiality. These categories are heuristic prioritization classifications rather than empirically calibrated risk estimates. Adversarial countermodel analysis Six bounded conceptual countermodels challenge potentially invalid equivalences: The absence of observation does not necessarily imply the impossibility of recovery. Perfect observation does not guarantee the existence of a safe recovery path. The absence of admissible actions does not imply nonexistence. A defined empty set is not identical to an undefined value. Operational terminality does not necessarily imply irreversible physical destruction. Exhaustive enumeration of finite subsets does not establish semantic completeness across all possible interactions. These countermodels are intended to expose hidden assumptions, clarify mathematical distinctions, and identify conditions requiring further proof. Terminal material closure protocol The publication specifies a seven-stage protocol requiring explicit scope declarations, evidence mapping, noncircular reasoning, independently checkable mathematical arguments, empirical validation for physical applications, rights and safety assurance, and transparent stopping conditions. The protocol distinguishes completeness of an obligation inventory from substantive discharge of its obligations. All 3,577 generated obligations are explicitly recorded as unresolved because the underlying combination register does not provide the individual proofs, operational specifications, or domain-specific empirical evidence required for their closure. Accordingly, the publication does not claim universal mathematical completeness, proof of every cross-domain relationship, discovery of new physical laws, or independently established astrophysical breakthroughs. Research continuity and interdisciplinary applications The broader archive preserves a cumulative research trajectory involving finite-state verification, stochastic transitions, partial observability, randomized recovery policies, model ambiguity, sensor costs, safety-recovery Pareto frontiers, and adversarial mathematical testing. Potential application domains include artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, stellar and plasma physics, fusion research, healthcare systems engineering, software and hardware reliability, institutional governance, legal accountability, and continuity of essential services. These applications are research directions and do not constitute validated deployment guarantees. Reproducibility and archived materials The Volume XXXV ZIP includes: The preserved Volume XXXIV ZIP archive. A mathematical appendix describing the material closure audit. A machine-readable CSV register of 3,577 obligations. A JSON results file containing counts, classifications, verification status, provenance information, and stopping conditions. A JSON file documenting six conceptual countermodels. Python source code used to generate and verify the bounded audit. The archive records seven structural assertions and two recovery checks executed during its verification workflow. Principal contribution The central contribution of Volume XXXV is a reproducible method for separating combinatorial completeness, materiality classification, adversarial counterexample analysis, and substantive evidentiary closure. It establishes a bounded inventory-completeness result while preserving explicit uncertainty about unproven mathematical relationships and unvalidated physical applications. Threshold Non-Circular Separate Final Closure The declared 511-combination, 3,577-obligation inventory is structurally complete. Substantive terminal material closure is not established. The stopping condition is reached because all declared obligations have assigned evidence statuses, while the proofs and independent measurements required to discharge them remain unavailable. This distinction is essential to maintaining noncircular reasoning, reproducibility, scientific falsifiability, and responsible interpretation across the integrated Continuity Science corpus.

The framework distinguishes the absence of a value, the existence of an empty set, the absence of an admissible continuation, and the disappearance of observable distinctions. These conditions are not assumed to be mathematically equivalent. The declared architecture contains nine foundational dimensions: States and spaces. Actions and transitions. Observations and information. Time and causality. Recovery and irreversibility. Safety and rights. Uncertainty and probability. Governance and recursion. Null-Void and terminal closure. The complete nonempty subset family of these nine dimensions contains 511 combinations, including 256 combinations containing the Null-Void dimension. Volume XXXV extends this combinatorial inventory by associating seven formal proof obligations with every combination, producing 3,577 material-obligation records. The resulting audit classifies 1,957 obligations as critical, 1,493 as high materiality, and 127 as medium materiality. These categories are heuristic prioritization classifications rather than empirically calibrated risk estimates. Adversarial countermodel analysis Six bounded conceptual countermodels challenge potentially invalid equivalences: The absence of observation does not necessarily imply the impossibility of recovery. Perfect observation does not guarantee the existence of a safe recovery path. The absence of admissible actions does not imply nonexistence. A defined empty set is not identical to an undefined value. Operational terminality does not necessarily imply irreversible physical destruction. Exhaustive enumeration of finite subsets does not establish semantic completeness across all possible interactions. These countermodels are intended to expose hidden assumptions, clarify mathematical distinctions, and identify conditions requiring further proof. Terminal material closure protocol The publication specifies a seven-stage protocol requiring explicit scope declarations, evidence mapping, noncircular reasoning, independently checkable mathematical arguments, empirical validation for physical applications, rights and safety assurance, and transparent stopping conditions. The protocol distinguishes completeness of an obligation inventory from substantive discharge of its obligations. All 3,577 generated obligations are explicitly recorded as unresolved because the underlying combination register does not provide the individual proofs, operational specifications, or domain-specific empirical evidence required for their closure. Accordingly, the publication does not claim universal mathematical completeness, proof of every cross-domain relationship, discovery of new physical laws, or independently established astrophysical breakthroughs. Research continuity and interdisciplinary applications The broader archive preserves a cumulative research trajectory involving finite-state verification, stochastic transitions, partial observability, randomized recovery policies, model ambiguity, sensor costs, safety-recovery Pareto frontiers, and adversarial mathematical testing. Potential application domains include artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, stellar and plasma physics, fusion research, healthcare systems engineering, software and hardware reliability, institutional governance, legal accountability, and continuity of essential services. These applications are research directions and do not constitute validated deployment guarantees. Reproducibility and archived materials The Volume XXXV ZIP includes: The preserved Volume XXXIV ZIP archive. A mathematical appendix describing the material closure audit. A machine-readable CSV register of 3,577 obligations. A JSON results file containing counts, classifications, verification status, provenance information, and stopping conditions. A JSON file documenting six conceptual countermodels. Python source code used to generate and verify the bounded audit. The archive records seven structural assertions and two recovery checks executed during its verification workflow. Principal contribution The central contribution of Volume XXXV is a reproducible method for separating combinatorial completeness, materiality classification, adversarial counterexample analysis, and substantive evidentiary closure. It establishes a bounded inventory-completeness result while preserving explicit uncertainty about unproven mathematical relationships and unvalidated physical applications. Threshold Non-Circular Separate Final Closure The declared 511-combination, 3,577-obligation inventory is structurally complete. Substantive terminal material closure is not established. The stopping condition is reached because all declared obligations have assigned evidence statuses, while the proofs and independent measurements required to discharge them remain unavailable. This distinction is essential to maintaining noncircular reasoning, reproducibility, scientific falsifiability, and responsible interpretation across the integrated Continuity Science corpus.

title: Jais 3: Introducing Arabic-centric Agentic AI
authors: Sheikh Khalid bin Khalifa Al Nahyan
abstract: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. For evaluation, we revisit how Arabic models are assessed, moving to fully generative evaluation on audited Arabic benchmarks. Across model sizes, Jais 3 matches or outperforms open-weight models of comparable size on Arabic and agentic benchmarks, with particularly strong agentic capabilities and Arabic instruction following, and far fewer hallucinations. We release the weights and the checkpoints from every training stage of all six models, together with samples of the training data, the data recipes and training configurations, the training logs, the audited benchmarks, and the evaluation code.

title: Zero-Shot Benchmarking of Unified Multimodal Models for Shallow-Water UAV Image Distortion Assessment and Restoration
abstract: Shallow-water UAV imagery provides centimeter-scale observations of benthic environments, but water-induced distortions complicate interpretation. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic zero-shot benchmark of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for both assessing water-induced distortions and restoring shallow-water imagery within the same model framework. We evaluate five open-weight unified MLLMs with frozen pretrained weights and without access to paired reference images or descriptions of the true seabed. The benchmark contains 1,000 image pairs: 600 semi-synthetic UAV scenes created by applying synthetic water distortions to real shallow-water imagery and 400 fully synthetic through-water scenes. Three independent human annotations cover five distortion types. We evaluate four assessment prompts (P0-P3), from direct instruction to structured task decomposition, on all 1,000 images and four diagnosis-guided restoration prompts (R0-R3) on a common 100-image subset. Assessment varies substantially by model and prompt, with systematic prediction biases and a best pooled balanced accuracy of 0.654 for distortion presence. The best pooled PSNR gain is +0.255 dB, no unified MLLM improves pooled LPIPS, and some outputs alter scene structure or hallucinate content. Two restoration-only baselines also show limited transfer: InstructIR achieves a pooled PSNR gain of +0.040 dB, while PromptFix degrades all four pooled metrics under every prompt. These results show that recognizing shallow-water degradation does not imply reliable physical restoration and provide a reproducible baseline for future work.

title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.

title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

title: Safety Is $Π_1$, Provability Is $Σ_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
abstract: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $Π_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $Σ_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $Σ_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $Π_1$ and not $Σ_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.

title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.

title: FTCircuitBench: A Benchmark Suite for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation and Architecture
abstract: Realizing large-scale quantum advantage is expected to require quantum error correction (QEC), making the compilation and optimization of logical operations a critical area of research. Logical computation imposes distinct constraints and operational paradigms that differ from those of the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) regime, motivating the continued evolution of compilation tools. Given the complexity of this emerging stack, where factors such as gate decomposition precision and computational models must be co-designed, standardized benchmarks and toolkits are valuable for evaluating progress. To support this need, we introduce FTCircuitBench, which serves as: (1) a benchmark suite of impactful quantum algorithms, featuring pre-compiled instances in both Clifford+T and Pauli Based Computation models; (2) a modular end-to-end pipeline allowing users to compile and decompose algorithms for various fault-tolerant architectures, supporting both prebuilt and custom optimization passes; and (3) a toolkit for evaluating the impact of algorithms and optimization across the full compilation stack, providing detailed numerical analysis at each stage. FTCircuitBench is fully open-sourced and maintained on GitHub.

title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
abstract: Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.

title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.
